holidays.name: Groundhog Day
holidays.description: Every year, a furry rodent is hauled out before crowds and cameras to predict whether winter will drag on for six more weeks. If he sees his shadow, it's more winter; if not, an early spring is on the way.
holidays.origin: Brought to Pennsylvania by German immigrants, who adapted a European Candlemas tradition in which a badger or hedgehog predicted the weather. The first official Groundhog Day in Punxsutawney was held in 1887.
holidays.funFact: Punxsutawney Phil's keepers claim he has lived for over 130 years thanks to a magical 'Groundhog Punch' elixir he sips every summer. Real groundhogs live only about 6 to 8 years in the wild.

holidays.name: National Tater Tot Day
holidays.description: A day devoted to the crispy, golden, bite-sized nuggets of grated potato that have been rescuing cafeteria lunches and casseroles for generations.
holidays.origin: Tater Tots were invented in 1953 by brothers F. Nephi and Golden Grigg, founders of Ore-Ida, who figured out how to use leftover potato slivers from cutting french fries. The unofficial holiday grew from fans' devotion to the snack.
holidays.funFact: The Grigg brothers reportedly sold 3 million pounds of Tater Tots in their first year, even though the name was meant to sound whimsical and fun.

holidays.name: World Wetlands Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate swamps, marshes, bogs, and other soggy ecosystems that filter water, protect coastlines, and host an astonishing amount of wildlife. It is basically a love letter to mud.
holidays.origin: It commemorates the signing of the Convention on Wetlands in Ramsar, Iran, on February 2, 1971. The United Nations officially recognized the day in 2021.
holidays.funFact: Wetlands cover only about 6 percent of Earth's land surface, yet they store roughly twice as much carbon as all the world's forests combined... a ratio that makes them true overachievers.

holidays.name: Candlemas
holidays.description: A centuries-old Christian feast when candles are blessed for the year ahead, often accompanied by weather lore and, in some places, a ceremonial eating of crepes.
holidays.origin: It marks the presentation of Jesus at the Temple 40 days after Christmas and has been celebrated since at least the 4th century. Later European folk traditions tied the day to weather prediction, which eventually inspired Groundhog Day.
holidays.funFact: In France, people celebrate by making crepes while holding a coin in one hand and flipping the pan with the other. If you flip it successfully, you're said to have prosperity for the year.

holidays.name: National Heavenly Hash Day
holidays.description: A sweet salute to the dessert-like mixture of chocolate, marshmallows, and nuts, often found in ice cream, candy, and old-school potluck salads.
holidays.origin: Heavenly hash is a Southern American dessert tradition with many regional variations, and its unofficial day is celebrated by dessert fans looking for an excuse to indulge.
holidays.funFact: Despite the name, there is no actual hash in it. Some versions of 'heavenly hash' are a fluffy fruit salad mixed with marshmallows and whipped cream, so the dish can be wildly different depending on the grandmother making it.
